name: Exodus Privacy
purpose: Platform that statically analyses Android applications to identify embedded trackers and requested permissions, publishing per-app reports and maintaining a public tracker database.
journalism_use_case: Establishing what an app actually does to its users: analyse a government service app, a state-promoted messaging app or a commercial app a story concerns, and show which tracking SDKs it embeds and what permissions it demands. For reporting on state apps that surveil citizens, this is the evidence base.
pros: Produces citable per-app reports with a named tracker list, which converts a vague privacy concern into a specific, checkable finding a reader can verify
The maintained tracker database is itself the asset: identifying an SDK as belonging to a particular data broker is the analytical step most reporters cannot do alone
AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, so you can analyse an app that the public instance has not covered or that you do not want to publicly request
Actively maintained (v1.33.0, 2026-09-13; pushed the same day) by a focused association with 820 stars
cons: Static analysis identifies embedded SDKs, not actual behaviour: an app may include a tracker it never activates, or exfiltrate data through code the analysis does not flag — so a report is evidence of capability rather than of conduct
Android only, so iOS apps (and therefore a large share of apps used in wealthier markets) are out of scope
Requesting an analysis on the public instance is a public act, disclosing your interest in a specific app — self-host if that matters
Tracker attribution depends on the database's completeness, so a novel or in-house tracking SDK will be missed or unnamed
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 820 stars with 52 open issues, release v1.33.0 (2026-09-13) with same-day push, AGPL-3.0. Exodus reports are widely cited in privacy journalism and advocacy, and the project publishes its methodology — note that session 1's URL for the tracker list (exodus-privacy.eu.org/en/page/trackers/) now 404s; the current entry point is the site root (verified 2026-11-17).
assessment: Adopt it as the first step in any story about an app's data practices, and pair it with dynamic analysis (mitmproxy) before publishing a claim about what an app sends — static presence of an SDK and observed transmission are different claims, and the stronger story uses both. For your profile the self-hosting option matters: if the app you are examining belongs to a government you are investigating, a public analysis request is a tip-off.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-13, latest release v1.33.0 published the same day, 820 stars, 52 open issues. Regular releases from an established association that also operates the public analysis service.
model_or_data_licence: The tracker database is published by the project; check its terms before redistributing the database itself.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted instance offered to users obliges source publication.
costs: No fee. Public instance free. Self-hosting estimate: a Django application plus static-analysis workers — one modest VM. Assumptions: occasional analysis volume.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps your analysis requests private. Using the public instance publishes the fact that an app was analysed, which discloses interest. The analysis itself involves no user data.
alternatives: MobSF for deeper static and dynamic app analysis you run yourself
mitmproxy to observe what an app actually transmits
Apktool for manual reverse engineering of a specific app
summary: Platform that statically analyses Android applications to identify embedded trackers and requested permissions…

name: Blacklight collector
purpose: Node library that loads a web page in an instrumented browser and records its tracking behaviour: third-party cookies, canvas fingerprinting, session recording, key logging, Facebook pixel and Google Analytics presence, and data flows to third parties.
journalism_use_case: The engine behind The Markup's Blacklight investigations: scan a set of websites — government services, hospitals, benefits portals, a political campaign — and report which of them send visitor data to advertising and analytics companies. It turns 'this site has trackers' into an enumerated, reproducible finding across hundreds of sites.
pros: Built by a newsroom for published investigations, so the measurements it takes are the ones that stand up editorially — session recording and key logging in particular are specific, explicable harms rather than abstract tracking
Dynamic measurement of actual behaviour, which is stronger evidence than static SDK detection: it records what the page really did when loaded
Scales to a survey: run it over hundreds of sites and you have a dataset, which is how the strongest tracker stories are built
GPL-3.0 and actively maintained (release 3.11.0, 2026-06-04; pushed 2026-09-03) with the methodology published alongside The Markup's investigations
cons: Measures a single page load from your vantage point, so results vary with geography, consent banners and A/B variation — a survey needs a documented, repeated methodology rather than one run
Your scanning traffic is visible to the target sites and to the tracking companies, so a large survey is detectable and your IP range may be flagged
Last push 2026-09-03 with the release in June: maintenance is steady but not brisk, and 245 stars means a small community for a tool this useful
Node/Puppeteer dependency surface and browser-version sensitivity, so reproducing a survey months later needs the environment pinned
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 245 stars with release @themarkup/blacklight-collector@3.11.0 (2026-06-04), pushed 2026-09-03, GPL-3.0. The Markup's published Blacklight investigations document the methodology and are the strongest evidence that the tool produces publishable findings. Session 1's candidate path mozilla/blacklight is a 404; the correct repository is the-markup/blacklight-collector (verified 2026-11-17).
assessment: Adopt it for any story about who is watching visitors to a set of websites — it is one of the clearest cases in this catalogue of a tool built for and proven by published journalism. For your profile the methodological work matters more than the running: define the site list, the vantage point, the consent-handling behaviour and the repetition schedule in advance, and publish them, because the finding's credibility rests on reproducibility. Pin the environment so you can re-run it a year later.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-03, latest release @themarkup/blacklight-collector@3.11.0 (2026-06-04), 245 stars, GPL-3.0. Two months since last push and five since release; steady newsroom-maintained tooling rather than a fast-moving project.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Tracker-identification lists it relies on may have their own sources.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: embedding in a distributed product triggers copyleft. Internal survey use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Compute for browser-based scanning — a survey of a few hundred sites is hours on one machine. Negligible infrastructure. Estimate.
privacy: Your scanning is visible to the target sites and to the trackers it triggers; it collects no personal data of your own. For a sensitive survey, scan from an egress not attributable to your newsroom.
alternatives: Exodus Privacy for the mobile-app equivalent
DuckDuckGo Tracker Radar as a reference dataset on tracker ownership and behaviour
OpenWPM for an academic-grade web-measurement platform
summary: Node library that loads a web page in an instrumented browser and records its tracking behaviour: third-party cookies…

name: DuckDuckGo Tracker Radar
purpose: Regularly regenerated dataset describing the most common third-party domains on the web: who owns them, what they do, their prevalence, fingerprinting behaviour and cookie usage.
journalism_use_case: The reference layer that turns a tracker domain into a named company: Blacklight tells you a site contacted a particular third-party domain, and Tracker Radar tells you which corporate entity owns it and what it does — which is the step that makes a story nameable rather than technical.
pros: Ownership attribution at scale is the specific gap it fills, and doing it yourself would mean weeks of corporate research per domain
Actively regenerated with dated releases (2026.11.10 on 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-16), so prevalence figures reflect the current web rather than a snapshot
Includes fingerprinting and cookie behaviour per domain, so you can characterise what a tracker does, not merely that it is present
Public and free to consult, backed by a company with a commercial interest in its accuracy
cons: LICENCE BLOCKER: the licence file states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — NonCommercial bars use by a commercially operated newsroom in a product or derived dataset, and ShareAlike means any derivative dataset you publish must carry the same licence. GitHub reports NOASSERTION, so scanners will not flag this

It is a dataset, not software, and should not be described as open-source tooling — the crawler that produces it (duckduckgo/tracker-radar-collector) is separately licensed and must be checked on its own terms
Coverage is of common third parties, so the obscure regional tracker on a government site in a smaller market may be absent
Ownership data ages as companies are acquired, so an attribution should be re-checked against corporate records before publication
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented fact, read from the licence blob on 2026-11-17: 'Licensed under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license... Note that this license does not apply to any DuckDuckGo logos or marks that may be contained in this repo.' Status is healthy: archived=false, release 2026.11.10, 1,749 stars (recorded in leads.md L7).
assessment: Use it as reference while reporting, and do not build it into a product or publish a derived dataset if your outlet is commercially operated — the NonCommercial and ShareAlike terms both bite, and 'we are journalism' does not satisfy NonCommercial. Practically: look up the ownership, verify it against corporate registries, and cite the registry in print. That keeps the finding defensible and sidesteps the licence entirely.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2026.11.10 (2026-11-10), 1,749 stars, SPDX NOASSERTION (actual: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 per the licence blob). Dated release cadence indicating regular regeneration.
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (licence blob read 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) — a DATASET licence, not a software licence
model_or_data_licence: Same. The producing crawler (duckduckgo/tracker-radar-collector) is separately licensed and was not assessed here.
licence_restrictions: NonCommercial: no commercial use without permission, which includes a commercially operated newsroom embedding it in a product. ShareAlike: derivative datasets must carry CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, which can contaminate a combined dataset you intend to publish. DuckDuckGo logos and marks are excluded from the licence.
costs: No fee for permitted non-commercial use. Commercial use requires permission — no published price. Negligible infrastructure (it is a git repository of JSON).
privacy: Static public data; consulting it discloses nothing.
alternatives: Corporate registry research to establish tracker ownership in a citable, licence-free way
Whotracks.me as an alternative tracker dataset with its own terms
EasyList/EasyPrivacy for blocklist-based identification without ownership data
blockers: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 — NonCommercial bars commercial productisation; ShareAlike propagates to derived datasets
summary: Regularly regenerated dataset describing the most common third-party domains on the web: who owns them, what they do…

name: MobSF (Mobile Security Framework)
purpose: Automated mobile application security framework performing static and dynamic analysis of Android, iOS and Windows apps, including code review, permission and API analysis, network traffic capture and malware checks.
journalism_use_case: The deep-analysis step when a story concerns a specific application: take the state-promoted contact-tracing app, the mandatory border app or a suspected stalkerware package and establish what it collects, which endpoints it contacts and what capabilities it holds — with dynamic analysis showing actual behaviour rather than declared permissions.
pros: Static plus dynamic analysis in one framework is the right combination for app investigation: static finds capability, dynamic shows conduct, and a story needs both
Covers iOS as well as Android, which closes the gap Exodus Privacy leaves
Outstanding maintenance for a tool of this complexity: release v4.6.6 (2026-11-15), pushed 2026-11-17, and only 2 open issues against 22,249 stars — an exceptional triage record
GPL-3.0 and self-hosted, so the app you are analysing and the fact you are analysing it stay private
cons: GPL-3.0 limits embedding in a proprietary newsroom product; immaterial for internal analysis but relevant if you build a service
Dynamic analysis requires an emulator or a real device and a working intercept setup, which is a meaningful operational commitment and the part that most often fails
Security-tooling orientation means output is dense and framed for penetration testers; translating it into a journalistic finding requires expertise
Analysing an app may breach its terms of service and, in some jurisdictions, reverse-engineering restrictions — a legal question to settle before starting, not after
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 22,249 stars with just 2 open issues, release v4.6.6 (2026-11-15), pushed 2026-11-17, GPL-3.0. The issue-throughput ratio is among the best in the catalogue and is strong evidence of active, disciplined maintenance.
assessment: Adopt where app investigation is a recurring need — the combination of maintenance quality, coverage and self-hosting makes it the strongest option in this subcategory. For your profile two practical points: get a legal view on reverse-engineering in your jurisdiction before you analyse a commercial or state app, and invest the setup time in dynamic analysis, because 'the app sent your location to this endpoint' is a far stronger published claim than 'the app requests location permission'.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v4.6.6 (2026-11-15), 22,249 stars, 2 open issues. Same-day commits, release within two days of the survey, near-zero backlog at very large scale.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Bundled signature and rule sets have their own sources.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: distributing a modified version or a product incorporating it triggers source obligations. Internal use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: a workstation or VM for static analysis plus an emulator or test device for dynamic analysis. Analyst time dominates. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely self-hosted, so neither the app binary nor your interest in it is disclosed to a third party — the key advantage over online app-scanning services.
alternatives: Exodus Privacy for fast Android tracker identification without a full analysis
Apktool plus manual review for targeted reverse engineering
mitmproxy alone to observe app traffic without full static analysis
blockers: Reverse-engineering an app may engage terms of service and local law — obtain a legal view first
summary: Automated mobile application security framework performing static and dynamic analysis of Android, iOS and Windows apps…

name: Apktool
purpose: Tool for reverse engineering Android APK files: decodes resources to near-original form, disassembles bytecode to smali, and can rebuild a modified APK.
journalism_use_case: Reading what an app actually contains: extract the hardcoded endpoints, API keys, strings and configuration from a surveillance or state app to show which servers it talks to and which third parties it embeds — often the most quotable evidence in an app investigation, because strings in a binary are hard to deny.
pros: Resource and string extraction gives concrete, quotable artefacts (endpoint URLs, provider names, hidden configuration) that make an app story specific
The foundational tool in this space — MobSF and most analysis pipelines depend on it — so understanding it underpins everything else
Apache-2.0 with excellent maintenance: release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), pushed 2026-11-16, 78 open issues against 27,258 stars
Mature and stable, so results are reproducible across versions — important when an analysis will be challenged
cons: Produces smali rather than readable source, so understanding logic (as opposed to extracting strings) requires real reverse-engineering skill
Obfuscated and packed apps resist analysis, and commercial spyware is typically heavily obfuscated — which is exactly the case you most want to analyse
Reverse engineering may breach terms of service and local law; the rebuild capability in particular can stray into territory you do not want to be in during an investigation
Narrow scope by design: it decodes, and everything analytical is yours to do
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 27,258 stars with 78 open issues, release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), pushed 2026-11-16, Apache-2.0. Its position as the standard APK decoder is evidenced by MobSF and the wider Android-analysis ecosystem depending on it.
assessment: Adopt as the low-level complement to MobSF — when you need to pull specific strings or configuration out of an APK, this is the tool, and the output is often the most publishable evidence in the story. For your profile the realistic expectation is that it works well on ordinary apps and poorly on deliberately obfuscated spyware; for the latter, the realistic route is a specialist partner (Amnesty Security Lab, Citizen Lab) rather than in-house analysis.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v3.0.3 (2026-07-20), 27,258 stars, 78 open issues. Long-running project with a consistent release history and a low backlog relative to scale.
licence_restrictions: None material for the tool. The legal constraints are external: reverse-engineering prohibitions in app terms and, in some jurisdictions, in law.
costs: No fee. Java runtime; negligible resources.
privacy: Entirely local decoding; the APK and your interest in it stay on your machine.
alternatives: MobSF for an automated analysis pipeline built on this
jadx for decompilation to more readable Java-like source
A specialist forensic partner for obfuscated commercial spyware
blockers: Reverse engineering may breach app terms and local law
summary: Tool for reverse engineering Android APK files: decodes resources to near-original form, disassembles bytecode to smali…

name: mitmproxy
purpose: Interactive TLS-capable intercepting HTTP(S) proxy with a console UI, web interface and Python scripting API, allowing inspection, modification and recording of traffic.
journalism_use_case: Showing what an app or device actually sends and to whom: put a phone behind mitmproxy, use the app, and record the endpoints, payloads and identifiers transmitted. 'This app sent your contacts to this company's servers' is a story; 'this app requests contacts permission' is not.
pros: Observed transmission is the strongest form of evidence in app and device investigation — it documents conduct rather than capability, and that is what makes a publishable claim
Python scripting API means you can automate capture and extraction across many apps or repeated sessions, turning a one-off demonstration into a survey
MIT licensed with outstanding maintenance (v12.3.1, 2026-10-25; pushed 2026-11-14) and a very large community (47,047 stars)
Local and self-contained: no cloud service, so the traffic you capture stays with you
cons: Requires installing a CA certificate on the device under test, which modern Android and iOS increasingly resist, and many apps use certificate pinning that defeats interception without further work (patching the app, which escalates the legal question)
Captured traffic contains credentials, tokens and personal data of whoever used the device — treat captures as highly sensitive and keep them briefly
Interception of a device you do not own, or of someone else's traffic, raises serious legal and ethical issues; this must be your own test device
560 open issues reflecting a broad feature surface; the learning curve for scripting is real
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 47,047 stars with 560 open issues, release v12.3.1 (2026-10-25), pushed 2026-11-14, MIT licence. mitmproxy is the standard tool for HTTP interception across security and development work, which is well established in its own documentation and ecosystem.
assessment: Adopt it — the capability to show what an app transmits is the single most valuable technical input to surveillance-industry reporting, and nothing else does it as well. For your profile the operating rules are: use a dedicated test device you own, never intercept a colleague's or source's live traffic, destroy captures promptly because they contain credentials, and expect certificate pinning to block the most interesting apps, at which point the realistic options are a specialist partner or a rooted test device with the legal position checked.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v12.3.1 (2026-10-25), 47,047 stars, 560 open issues. Frequent releases on a 12.x line with a broad contributor base and long-term stability.
licence_restrictions: None material. The constraints are legal rather than licensing: intercepting traffic you are not authorised to intercept is unlawful in most jurisdictions.
costs: No fee. A test device and a workstation; negligible infrastructure.
privacy: All capture is local. The sensitivity runs the other way: captures contain credentials and personal data from the test session, so storage, access and retention need the same care as source material.
alternatives: MobSF's dynamic analysis, which wraps interception into an app-analysis workflow
Wireshark for lower-level packet capture where HTTP is not the layer of interest
Frida for defeating certificate pinning — which escalates the legal and technical commitment
blockers: Certificate pinning blocks interception for many apps; intercepting traffic you are not authorised to intercept is unlawful
summary: Interactive TLS-capable intercepting HTTP(S) proxy with a console UI, web interface and Python scripting API…
